speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. To better understand your symptoms, could you please describe how long each episode of dizziness lasts and whether you experience any accompanying symptoms like hearing loss, tinnitus, or nausea?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Given the sudden, position-dependent nature of your vertigo, have you noticed any new hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or tinnitus specifically triggered by these episodes? Also, have you experienced any double vision, limb numbness, or difficulty walking during these spells?

REQUEST TEST: Audiogram; REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike maneuver results.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Audiometry: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with presbycusis. No sudden drops in hearing indicative of Meniere's disease or labyrinthitis. Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: Doctor: I see a previous doctor suspected migraine, but your description of strictly position-dependent spinning is highly characteristic of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). Have you noticed if these spells are triggered specifically by rolling over in bed, looking up, or bending down? REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike maneuver results; REQUEST IMAGES: Oculomotor exam video.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV. Oculomotor Exam Video: Normal vestibular response with the exception of response elicited during Dix-Hallpike maneuver, consistent with BPPV. No evidence of central lesions or infarcts on MRI Brain.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), likely Right Posterior Canal involvement. This is confirmed by your position-dependent symptoms, positive Dix-Hallpike test with right-sided nystagmus, and normal MRI ruling out central causes. Treatment will involve canalith repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver).
